title: Pattern Drafter Updates | Clo 2026.0 Features Deep Dive
description:
The new update to our Pattern Drafter in CLO 2026.0 allows you to automatically generate POMs and apply grading simply by entering measurements during pattern drafting, with flexible and intuitive editing capabilities.
Check out other new features here:https://clo3d.com/en/clo/features

markdown_content: ## Pattern Drafter Tool: Where to Find It and How to Start This section explains how to open Pattern Drafter from the top toolbar and begin a drafting workflow using a selected pattern type (e.g., shirt with set-in sleeves). It also covers the auto-arrange/sew behavior when an avatar is present in the 3D window. - Open **Pattern Drafter** from the **top toolbar** under **2D**. - Select **Pattern Drafter** to open the drafting window. - If you have an **avatar** in your **3D window**, anything you create in Pattern Drafter can be **automatically arranged and sewn**, reducing extra steps. - Choose a **pattern type**: - Example: **Shirt** - A **shirt** can also be used as a **dress** depending on how it’s drafted. - Select sleeve style: - Example used: **Set-in sleeve** - Not using **raglan** or **drop shoulder**. - Draft example mentioned: - A **long sleeve shirt** in a **tunic-like**/long style (shirt that “covers anything for the body,” i.e., extended length). ## Measurements Setup and AI-Assisted Measurement Generation This section covers how Pattern Drafter populates measurements, what to do if AI measurement generation is unavailable (grayed out), and how to use an AI tool to create measurements from an image. - Measurement population: - Measurements are automatically populated in the measurement page once drafting starts. - Reminder: If you don’t have your own specs/measurements and only have a **sketch/drawing**, you can use an **AI tool** to generate measurements. - If the AI tool is **grayed out**, it needs to be **activated**. - The speaker references a separate video that explains how AI works and how to activate it. - AI workflow: - Open/select the AI measurement tool. - **Bring in an image**. - The tool **automatically creates measurements**. ## Choosing Drafting Complexity: General vs. Simple This section explains the difference between **General** and **Simple** drafting options and how scrolling updates the pattern in real time. It also highlights the role of the **ClO algorithm** in reducing manual uncertainty. - The speaker prefers **General** because they often work from: - a **spec sheet** - known **measurements** - more **control** - **Simple** option: - Fewer measurements to manage. - Useful for users who don’t know all measurements or designers who want control over only key inputs. - Interaction: - Use the **mouse scroll** to move through options. - The pattern updates accordingly on the right. - Algorithm support: - The **ClO algorithm** does much of the work. - If you’re unsure, you can preview the result and adjust until satisfied. - Actions: - **Create** to generate the drafted pattern. - **Preview** (optional) to view without committing. - **Simulate** to see how garments look quickly. ## Reset and Re-Enter Measurements for a Specific Draft This section describes resetting back to defaults and then importing measurement values for a custom build—especially via an Excel-based “open folder” workflow. - Reset behavior: - Use **Reset** to return to the original/default measurements. - Measurement import workflow: - The speaker uses **Open folder** because measurements are saved in an **Excel sheet**. - They open a **“deep dive chart”** that is **automatically populated** based on what’s configured in Pattern Drafter. - Editing measurement values: - Example capability: change lengths such as high/low adjustments (e.g., “this is actually 28… I want this to be a high-low… 25”). - Avoid double work: - Recommended practice: - Save/export the **default** measurement set. - Modify measurements as needed. - Reuse these in **tech packs**. - Import requires the measurement list to match the expected setup (the speaker emphasizes the list must align with the tool’s expected measurement names/order). - Version note: - Most basics have existed since **2022**, even though algorithms/features were updated more recently. - Measurement types reminder: - **Total measurements** (icon mentioned): - Account for **front + back**. - Example: **Across bust** total equals the combined front and back measurement. - **Half measurements**: - Used when total measurements aren’t provided. - Example: across the body is represented as a half/full-half structure. - **Quarter measurements**: - Used for certain dimensions (example mentioned: **shoulder slope/drop** described as a quarter measurement component). ## Layout Controls: Symmetry, Visible Lines, and Measurement Selection This section explains how symmetry and measurement visibility affect the drafting layout, plus how to use settings to choose which measurements to use (letting the algorithm fill in the rest). - Symmetry: - Default shown: **half symmetry** for a regular shirt layout. - Option: switch to **symmetry** to cut the pattern in half symmetrically. - Option: **turn off symmetry** if needed. - Line visibility: - There are **line options** to turn on/off measurement-related lines that may otherwise be hidden. - Measurement settings icon: - Opens a **full list** of measurements. - You can **check on/off** which measurements to use. - Smart algorithm behavior vs. strict rules: - If you want the algorithm to copy/derive values: - Turn off certain back measurements so the tool uses front/body logic. - Examples of “don’t rewrite, let ClO figure it out”: - If **across shoulder** is turned off for the back, the algorithm can copy the front across-shoulder logic. - If **across waist** differs, the speaker describes setting it so back across-waist matches the front across-waist unless otherwise required. - If you want strict control: - Turn on all measurements and manually write everything in. - Additional drafting details: - Example mentioned: adding **cuffs** or a **front hem/back hem** using drop-down options after drafting a straight-up base pattern. - Measurement reference points: - Drop-downs choose where lengths are measured from (example used: **high point shoulder** for length). - Other reference options include **center front** (mentioned as an available option). ## Pattern Drafter Update: Grading via a Grading Measurement Table This section covers the new **grading** capability in Pattern Drafter, including how to define a **base size** and add grading rules for sizes like XS–XL. It also includes unit behavior (inches in the example) and guidance on how to avoid incorrect rule direction. - New grading feature: - A **grading icon** appears in the updated interface. - When selected, you can add grading using a **grading measurement table**. - Example grading set: - **Five graded sizes**: **Extra Small, Small, Medium, Large, Extra Large** - Base size concept: - The measurements shown in the grading table correspond to a chosen **base size**. - Example: measurements match **Medium**, so **Medium** is selected as the **base size**. - Grading rules are applied relative to the base size. - Rule entry options: - Using **deltas** (differences): - For example, from **Medium to Small**: enter a rule like **10 centimeters / 0.5 inch / 1/8 inch / 10 millimeters** (speaker mentions these as possible unit expressions). - Units used in the software determine what you should type. - Using **absolute measurements**: - If you know a size’s actual measurement (e.g., **Large length is 29 inches instead of 28.5**), you can type the actual value. - Sign behavior (relative to base size): - In the speaker’s example, since base is **Medium**: - Sizes **below Medium** naturally become **negative** unless you override by entering actual values. - Sizes **above Medium** become **positive**. - Guidance to avoid mistakes: - The speaker demonstrates a “how you can get it wrong” scenario for **neck width**: - Example issue: the table interprets how you reference the measurement column/row (speaker explains it may pull from the wrong adjacent reference). - Best practice emphasized: - Work **from the base size outward** (middle to outer sizes). - This prevents rule interactions where deltas can collapse to zero due to referencing the wrong source row. - Practical example values (as stated): - **Length**: - Most sizes: **28** - **Extra Large**: increase by **0.5** (half an inch) so it becomes **29**. - **Neck width**: - The speaker targets increments of **0.125** (1/8 inch) using base-out logic. - **Shoulder slope/cross shoulder**: - The speaker notes a correction: - shoulder slope should be **0.25** (they adjust it after a quick check). - Sleeve grading: - For sleeve-related rules, the speaker switches to using **measurement columns** (rather than plus/minus columns) while entering grading values. - Rule updates: - As grading values are entered, the table updates **automatically**. - Direction of entry:

It also includes unit behavior (inches in the example) and guidance on how to avoid incorrect rule direction. - New grading feature: - A **grading icon** appears in the updated interface. - When selected, you can add grading using a **grading measurement table**. - Example grading set: - **Five graded sizes**: **Extra Small, Small, Medium, Large, Extra Large** - Base size concept: - The measurements shown in the grading table correspond to a chosen **base size**. - Example: measurements match **Medium**, so **Medium** is selected as the **base size**. - Grading rules are applied relative to the base size. - Rule entry options: - Using **deltas** (differences): - For example, from **Medium to Small**: enter a rule like **10 centimeters / 0.5 inch / 1/8 inch / 10 millimeters** (speaker mentions these as possible unit expressions). - Units used in the software determine what you should type. - Best practice emphasized: - Work **from the base size outward** (middle to outer sizes). - This prevents rule interactions where deltas can collapse to zero due to referencing the wrong source row. -
